Philosophical readings

Use this guide to locate the intellectual sources behind Yinyang's arguments. The reading map locates the arguments themselves; this page explains which originals bear on them and where an interpretation extends its source. Select by question and read the relevant passage in context. These sources neither supply a personal portrait nor establish a psychological mechanism.

Heraclitus: fire, measure, and opposing tension

B6 concerns the daily-new Sun, B30 fire and measure, and B51 bow and lyre. B2 and B50 provide the wider context for logos beyond an individual speaker. Daniel W. Graham's scholarly account, especially sections 3–4, explains disputed readings of fire, unity, and opposition.

The stealing-fire essay draws on this lineage to understand persistence and change, organizing activity histories as event streams. It does not attribute a modern computational ontology or formal calculus to Heraclitus. Whether the historical Heraclitus was a fire monist remains disputed. Yinyang adopts contemporary fire monism to express the world's becoming and transformation; computational ontology constructs process representations through objects, events, states, and relations. World, process, and expression connects that understanding with naturalism, shared physical realization, and computational representation; B30 does not establish a modern physical theory. Paraconsistent Logic explains non-explosive consequence and its difference from dialetheism: tolerating inconsistent information need not declare contradictions true.

Yinyang and Taiji

Zhou Dunyi's Taijitu shuo connects movement and stillness through mutual grounding and continuing transformation. Xici, upper connects change with ongoing generation; Xici, lower offers the Sun and Moon producing illumination through their reciprocal movement.

Mutual becoming through Yinyang and Taiji quotes and develops these Zhou Dunyi and Xici passages. Zhuangzi, Tian Zifang connects interaction, harmony, and generation as additional reading. Its fish-body/eye distinction is a contemporary interpretation of roles and actual participants, not the sole historical meaning or an identification of the familiar Shuang yu with Zhou's original diagram. The Yinyang and Taiji essay places the Sun–Moon–Earth relation within this movement: Sun and Moon express differentiated generation, reception, and shaping. Person and model are actual participants whose emphases can be retained or exchanged; Earth is the answering material and shared living environment.

Hegel: sublation, history, and spirit

The Encyclopaedia Logic, §§79–81, and the development of §82 present understanding, dialectic, and speculation as connected moments: fixing determinations, examining their own limitations, and grasping affirmative content within opposition. They inform the reading of consistent views and common consequences. Repair semantics retains its own definitions; the philosophical comparison asks how difference contributes to commonality.

The Preface to the Phenomenology of Spirit, paragraph 18, offers the thought of return to self through otherness, developed here in the dialectical meaning of role change as an interpretation of finite cooperation. The Introduction, paragraphs 84–86, examines changes in knowledge, object, and criterion through experience. The account of premises and philosophical models uses it to question the concepts organizing judgment. Read alongside Lacan's dialectical reversal to compare return through the other, revision of criteria, and changes of subjective position.

Science of Logic, “Being,” §§184–187 develops cessation and preservation in sublation. Query rewriting and sublation uses this relation for a bounded comparison with query rewriting; a technical equivalence does not prove a thesis about Hegel's whole dialectic.

The Introduction to the Philosophy of History, part III connects spirit's self-knowledge with freedom and world history. The Philosophy of Spirit, §§553–564 locates absolute spirit relative to subjective and objective spirit and develops art within that account. World, process, and expression keeps these categories distinct from generic stages of a feedback loop.

Wittgenstein: pictures and philosophical therapy

Read Philosophical Investigations, Part I, §§109, 115, and 133 together. The link supplies the German original; section numbers let readers locate the same remarks in a translation.

Passage What to attend to
§109 How examining language and describing its use can work on a philosophical difficulty. Ask which relation becomes clearer when an apparent demand is described in context.
§115 How a picture embedded in language can hold thought captive. Ask what a description makes seem inevitable and which alternatives it hides.
§133 Why philosophical work admits different methods compared to therapies, and how clarification can make it possible to stop. Ask what has changed when the original problem loses its grip.

The fire essay applies this route to pictures of obligatory frontier pursuit and returns their demands to surrounding life. That application belongs to this collection. Personal understanding then distinguishes clarifying concepts such as ability or progress from proposing a psychological explanation of a person's activity. The two can inform one another without a convincing description settling an empirical claim.

Buddhist reading: fire, cessation, and crossing

Begin with the Fire Sermon, Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.28 and the Nibbāna Sutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya 38.1. The former describes senses, consciousness, contact, and feeling as burning with passion, aversion, and delusion, then develops dispassion and release. The latter identifies nirvana with the ending of those three and points to the noble eightfold path. Both links give Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu's translations.

Ask what is burning and what ceases. How might developing a capability and loosening grasping support one another, and why are they not equivalent? Borrowed fire and nirvana connects knowledge and creative capability with examining desire, habit, and self-image. Buddhist liberation thus participates in reflection on cultivation's purpose; the contrast between these two meanings of fire is this work's construction.

Read the water-snake and raft passages together in the Alagaddūpama Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 22, translated by Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu. The sections “The Water-snake Simile” and “The Raft Simile” locate the relevant portions of the discourse. The translator's introduction and notes are commentary accompanying the translated text.

The water-snake passage concerns how a teaching is grasped and understood; the raft passage follows a traveler who builds and uses a raft to cross, then considers whether to keep carrying it. Read the complete movement: what the means makes possible, how it is used, and when carrying it becomes an unnecessary burden. This gives “letting go” a situation and a purpose.

The raft connects the preceding question of purpose with means: tools, conceptual models, and the little-fire self-image can contribute to life, remain revisable, and be released when their work is done. These three discourses supply the specific sources for this dialogue. Creative cultivation is the work's contemporary development, while nirvana retains the liberative meaning stated in the discourses. This reading path leaves room for further inquiry rather than summarizing Buddhist traditions.

Nietzsche: three metamorphoses and creation

Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Part One, “The Three Metamorphoses” presents bearing, negation, and new creation through the camel, lion, and child. What kind of person do we want to cultivate? — Baby Heraclitus already draws on this line: the child concerns beginning and creating anew, not abandoning judgment or prescribing stages everyone must complete.

James and Bergson: the stream of thought and duration

Author and original work Connection in the collection
William James, The Principles of Psychology, chapter IX, “The Stream of Thought” Change, continuity, personal character, and selection in thought. Forming a life trajectory uses this to examine experiential continuity while distinguishing present experience, retained records, and working models.
Henri Bergson, Time and Free Will, chapter II Duration and measurable, spatialized time. The collection's distinctions among clock time, experiential rhythms, and update order enter into dialogue with this account without equating them.

Freud: negation and acceptance

Freud's “Negation” (1925), pp. 1–3 distinguishes intellectual recognition and acceptance in an analytic account. Its interpretive inversions do not license treating ordinary denial as admission.

Lacan: enunciation, retroaction, and singular creation

Lacan brings three connected questions to this collection: how people acquire a position through language and images, how later speech changes the meaning of earlier expression, and how singular practices participate in a person's mode of existence. The site develops these questions into contemporary accounts of personal understanding, model collaboration, and the sinthome.

Conceptual explanations, examples, formal translations, and original-text references are gathered in A guide to Lacanian concepts: from original texts to personal practice. Its dialectical reading follows recognition, desire, and speech before comparing them with model revision. The guide also develops the Other, the divided subject, retroaction, the three registers, and the sinthome, distinguishing the original concepts from this site's extensions.

Fire myths: Prometheus, Kuafu, and living together

Prometheus is a mythic figure; Hesiod and Plato supply different texts through which this collection encounters him. Hesiod's Theogony, lines 507–616 gives fire theft and its carrier a narrative form. Shan Hai Jing, Haiwai Beijing supplies Kuafu's pursuit. Stealing fire and cultivating creative capacity compares pursuing overwhelming power with bringing usable capacities into a finite life.

Plato's Protagoras, 320c–322d places the myth in Protagoras's account of civic learning: arts and fire are followed by reverence and justice shared by all. Plato is the dialogue's author, Protagoras a thinker represented within it, and Prometheus a character in its myth. The fire essay takes their relation as a comparison between technical means and purposes of living together. Its AI application is a contemporary argument, rather than a claim about an ancient prediction.

Deleuze and Guattari: connections, production, and becoming

The independently authored Machines and becoming essay reads Anti-Oedipus, chapter 1 and chapter 4's first positive task of schizoanalysis, alongside A Thousand Plateaus, plateaus 4 and 6. Desiring-machines open the question of what connections produce; assemblages bring bodies and expression into view. The essay distinguishes a process of becoming from a clinical condition and treats its songwriting and harness examples as contemporary comparisons. This provides a neighboring question to the sinthome essay: through what connections can an established personal practice arrangement produce new capacities?

Personal practice: Bruner, Foucault, Hobbes, and Mill

Bruner's Life as Narrative and Foucault's Technologies of the Self inform Stealing fire and cultivating creative capacity's connection between self-expression, continuing practice, and change. Narrative can organize later understanding; writing and relations with others can participate in self-transformation. The model-supported extension belongs to this collection.

Personal-first humanism also reads Hobbes's Leviathan, chapter IV on names and particular things, and Mill's On Liberty, chapter III on individuality and experiments of living. These sources clarify the questions of description and plural coexistence. The present personal-first orientation remains a separately argued choice.

Inquiry and frameworks: Peirce, Dewey, Carnap, and Feng Ye

Reasoning uses Peirce's 1908 manuscript MS 841 to distinguish explanatory hypotheses, experiential consequences, and assessment. Embodied experimental philosophy reads Dewey's Reconstruction in Philosophy, chapters IV–V: experience includes acting and undergoing consequences. Together these routes give inquiry room to propose, act, return, and revise.

Carnap's Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology distinguishes questions within a framework from its practical adoption. Finite inquiry and abstraction compares this collection's question-relative account with Professor Feng Ye's Studies in No-Self Physicalism, especially §§1.1, 6.5, and 7.4.2. Their shared methodological questions about finite understanding and representation do not establish identical accounts of physical realization. Yinyang adopts one physical reality as its common ground while using question-relative abstraction; particular reductions and bridge assumptions require their own support. Compare the actual arguments rather than inferring either agreement or disagreement from their labels.

Will, irrationality, and self-conflict: Frankfurt, Davidson, Mele, and Holton

These philosophers give conflict more specific objects: desire and endorsement, resolve and later inclination, evidence and motivation, and a person's interpretation of themselves. They are supplementary entrances, not proof that the collection accepts one shared architecture of mind.

Philosopher and original Central question
Harry Frankfurt, Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person (1971) How does wanting something differ from wanting a particular desire to become one's effective motive? First-order desires and second-order volitions offer one analysis of conflict.
Donald Davidson, Paradoxes of Irrationality (1982); Deception and Division (reprinted in the 2004 collection) How can reasons, causes, and mental partitioning help explain irrationality and self-deception? Partitioning is an explanatory proposal to compare with alternatives.
Alfred R. Mele, Real Self-Deception (1997) Must self-deception involve intentional self-deception or simultaneous contrary beliefs? Examine motivationally biased evidence processing and the accompanying commentaries and reply.
Richard Holton, Intention and Weakness of Will (1999); What Is the Role of the Self in Self-Deception? (2001) Resolve, premature abandonment, reasonable reconsideration after conditions change, and understanding one's own beliefs. Author-manuscript pagination may differ from the journals.

For conflict in experience, relationships, and therapy, continue to psychological readings.

Lakoff, Johnson, and Gentner: metaphor and relational analogy

George Lakoff and Mark Johnson's Metaphors We Live By, chapters 1–3 concerns metaphor in everyday conceptual life. Dedre Gentner's Structure-Mapping (1983) makes relational mapping explicit. Writing a personal philosophy through literary programming and From personal philosophy to personal models already use these resources. Metaphor gives understanding a form; particular analogical inferences still need checking.

Mind, knowledge, and explanation

Clark and Chalmers's The Extended Mind informs Stealing fire and cultivating creative capacity's account of active environmental supports. From personal philosophy to personal models connects that question with Hollan, Hutchins, and Kirsh's distributed-cognition research: understanding can develop across people, models, records, and tools.

Varela, Evan Thompson, and Eleanor Rosch's The Embodied Mind (1991) brings cognitive science, lived experience, and contemplative practice together; Shared reflection and continued cultivation already uses it to examine embodied participation. Hollan, Hutchins, and Kirsh's Distributed Cognition (2000) supplies the original account of cognition across people, artifacts, and time.

Joshua Knobe and Shaun Nichols's An Experimental Philosophy Manifesto (2008) introduces an empirical research orientation; the linked author-hosted file is a proof. Embodied experimental philosophy distinguishes this tradition from personal philosophical experimentation through making, participation, and reflection.

Gordana Dodig-Crnkovic's Information, Computation, Cognition (2013) is another natural-philosophical resource already used in Stealing fire and cultivating creative capacity: informational structure, computational dynamics, and agency across levels. It neighbors embodied, extended, and distributed cognition without being the same theory or establishing that human experience is a digital algorithm.

For psychological processes, empirical assessment, belief, and interaction, continue to psychological readings. Their theories and evidence investigate how knowing actually happens; philosophy continues to ask about explanation, grounds for knowledge, and the scope of mind.

Technical sources for the Gödel Machine and Darwin Gödel Machine appear in engineering readings. Preference harness retains its philosophical comparisons while preserving the assumptions and scope of formal repair, inference, and query transformation.

Source scope

These links preserve the public intellectual sources and their conceptual limits. Personal evidence and the history of adopting or revising an interpretation remain in the situated package's source account. The reading map does not replace reading the passages that matter to an actual argument.
